chapter_theme: The patikam tells how Puhar got its two names, from the goddess Champa and from the Kaveri released by Agastya, then runs through the whole story from the festival and the prince's pursuit to the bowl, the prison made a house of charity, the hearing of the schools and Manimekalai's vow in Kanchi to end rebirth; its colophon has Saathan recite the thirty songs of her renunciation to a listening Ilango.

the immortal sage who overturned his water-pot to release the Kaveri
the Chola king of the sun's line whose request brought the Kaveri
Madhavi's mother, a courtesan of Puhar
Madhavi's attendant
the dancer of Puhar, Manimekalai's mother, now a Buddhist renunciant

the Chola prince of Puhar who pursues Manimekalai
the sea goddess, Kovalan's family deity, who carries Manimekalai to Manipallavam
Manimekalai's companion, left asleep in the Uvavanam garden

the Buddhist teacher of Puhar, later in Kanchi
the earlier owner of the bowl, reborn as king of a land across the sea
the goddess who gave the bowl to Aputhiran
the chaste wife of Puhar (named Aathirai later in the epic) who puts the first food in the bowl

manimekalai:0:1-18.reading: The narrator tells how Champa, the shining goddess of this island who came south from the golden mountain and did austerity against the asuras for the sake of the suffering earth, dwelt under the jambu tree at Champapati, and how, when a Chola king of the sun's line asked for water, Agastya overturned his pot and the Kaveri flowed east to that city, where the old ascetic goddess welcomed her as a lamp come to quench a long desire.
manimekalai:0:1-18.nuance: The patikam opens not with the heroine but with the founding of Puhar's two names, so the city of the epic is first a goddess's seat. Lines 10 (கஞ்ச வேட்கையின்) and 17-18 (ஆணு விசும்பின் ஆகாயகங்கை வேணவாத் தீர்த்த விளக்கே) are hard: whether the Ganga of the sky is the one whose desire is quenched or a title given to the Kaveri is not clear from the words.
manimekalai:0:1-18.event: Agastya, at a Chola king's request, overturns his water-pot; the Kaveri flows to Champapati and the goddess Champa welcomes her.

manimekalai:0:19-31.unit_note: Boundary moved: the core units 1-18, 19-34 and 35-50 are recut here to 19-31 and 32-50, since the welcome scene closes with Champa's blessing நீ வாழிய! என at line 31, and line 32 opens the catalogue of the story's events (-ததும்) that runs to the end.
manimekalai:0:19-31.reading: Agastya bids the river bow to the old ascetic goddess; the Kaveri, the Chola banner who never fails her course though the planets stray and summer lengthens, bows, and Champa takes her to her lap and gives the old city, named for herself since Brahma's creation, the river's name as well.
manimekalai:0:19-31.nuance: This is how the patikam accounts for the city's two names (இரு பால் பெயரிய, line 32): Champapati and the Kaveri's city. The river is called the daughter of the Cholas of the unbending sceptre, so the land's fertility is tied to the dynasty's justice from the first page.
manimekalai:0:19-31.event: At Agastya's word the Kaveri bows to Champa, who takes her on her lap and names the city after her.

manimekalai:0:32-50.unit_note: Boundary moved from 34/35 to 31/32: the core unit 35-50 began in mid-sentence (பெருகியது அலர் என at 34 is the thought of சித்திராபதி at 35). This unit runs from the festival announcement at 32 to the knowledge of former births at 50, closed by உணர்ந்ததும்.
manimekalai:0:32-50.reading: The patikam begins its summary of the story: Indra's festival is proclaimed in the twice-named city; Chitrapathi, stung that the town's gossip grows, sends word to Madhavi through Vasantamalai; Manimekalai goes to the garden for flowers, sees the prince, hides in the crystal chamber, and he leaves troubled; the goddess Manimekala carries her to Manipallavam and wakes Sutamati; alone on the island she grieves, and at a shining jewel seat she comes to know all her former births.
manimekalai:0:32-50.nuance: The summary names the jewel seat (மணிப் பீடிகை) only by its light; that it is the Buddha's seat is left to kaathai 9 onward. The knowledge of former births (பழம் பிறப்பு) is given as an event, not argued, and it is the turn on which the whole renunciation rests.
manimekalai:0:32-50.event: Manimekalai flees the prince into the crystal chamber, is carried by the goddess to Manipallavam, and there learns her former births at the jewel seat.

manimekalai:0:51-68.unit_note: Boundary moved from 67/68 to 68/69: line 67 (அம்பலம் அடைந்தனள் ஆய் இழை என்றே) is the report that brings the prince at line 68 (கோமகன் சென்றதும்), so the sentence ends at 68.
manimekalai:0:51-68.reading: The summary continues: the goddess gives her a mantra and bids her cease grieving; Deepatilakai gives her the great bowl; with her mothers she bows to the teacher Aravanar, who tells her of Aputhiran and of how Chinta Devi gave him the bowl; she carries it into the city's street for alms, a chaste wife puts the first food in it, she ends Kayachandigai's elephant-fire hunger, and when she goes to the public hall the prince follows.
manimekalai:0:51-68.nuance: The bowl passes from goddess to Aputhiran to Manimekalai, and its first food comes from a பத்தினி (line 64), so the epic's charity starts from a chaste wife's gift; the heroine who renounced the courtesan's life receives first from the epic's figure of wifely virtue. The begging renunciant is the one who ends another's hunger.
manimekalai:0:51-68.event: Manimekalai receives the bowl, hears its history from Aravanar, begs in Puhar, is first fed by a chaste wife, and ends Kayachandigai's hunger.

manimekalai:0:69-88.unit_note: Boundary moved from 87/88 to 88/89: line 87 ('நவை அறு நன்பொருள் உரைமினோ' என) is her request to the schools and line 88 (சமயக் கணக்கர் தம் திறம் கேட்டதும்) completes it.
manimekalai:0:69-88.reading: The summary goes on: in Kayachandigai's form Manimekalai turns the king's prison into a house of charity; Kanchanan, taking her for his wife, kills the prince with his sword; she, grieving, is calmed by a divine voice; the king orders her imprisoned and then freed; she teaches dharma to the queen, goes to Aputhiran's land and with him to Manipallavam, takes an ascetic's form in Vanji, and asks the schools' reckoners to state the truth.
manimekalai:0:69-88.nuance: Line 72 sets the epic's justice theme in one turn: a prison of the war-making king (மறம் செய் வேலோன்) becomes a house of dharma (அறம் செய் கோட்டம்). Whom she teaches at line 81 is not named: நறு மலர்க் கோதை is read here as the queen, since 58 used the same phrase for Manimekalai as hearer and here she is the teller. The patikam says she heard (கேட்டதும்) the schools, not that she refuted them.
manimekalai:0:69-88.event: Manimekalai frees the prison, Kanchanan kills the prince, the king jails and releases her, and she travels to Aputhiran's land, Manipallavam and Vanji, where she hears the schools.

manimekalai:0:89-98.unit_note: Boundary moved from 87/88 to 88/89 (see 69-88); the unit begins with the journey to Aravanar in Kanchi.
manimekalai:0:89-98.reading: The summary ends: with her mothers she seeks out Aravanar and enters Kanchi, casts off her borrowed form and bows at his feet, takes up the ascetic life, hears the dharma and vows that the round of becoming be cut; and the colophon says that Saathan, the grain merchant, with Ilango the prince graciously listening, set out Manimekalai's renunciation in thirty songs.
manimekalai:0:89-98.nuance: The epic's title theme is given at line 97 as மணிமேகலை துறவு, and its count as ஆறு ஐம் பாட்டு (thirty). The roles of the Silappathikaram's patikam are reversed: there Ilango composes and Saathan hears; here Saathan composes and Ilango hears. Whether this colophon is the poet's own or a later frame the text does not say.
manimekalai:0:89-98.event: Manimekalai finds Aravanar in Kanchi, bows to him, takes up austerity and vows to end rebirth; Saathan recites the work before Ilango.

claims.claim: taking up austerity and hearing the dharma lead to the cutting off of becoming

links.note: Silappathikaram's patikam ends with Ilango graciously telling and Saathan the grain merchant hearing (அடிகள் அருள ... சாத்தன் கேட்டனன்); Manimekalai's ends with Ilango graciously hearing and Saathan setting out the work (இளங்கோ வேந்தன் அருளிக் கேட்ப ... சாத்தன் ... அறிய வைத்தனன்), each in thirty parts.
links.teaches: The two patikams frame the twin epics as one exchange between the same two men, each the listener of the other's poem, so the tradition joins them by their frames and not only by Madhavi's daughter continuing the story.

links.note: Pattinappalai opens on the Kaveri that does not fail though the white star strays south and the sky withholds rain; the patikam calls the Kaveri the Tamil maiden who does not leave her course though the planets stray and summer lengthens (கோள் நிலை திரிந்து கோடை நீடினும் தான் நிலை திரியா).
links.teaches: The epic takes the Sangam praise-formula for Puhar's river and turns it into a person, a Chola daughter who bows to the city's goddess and gives the city its second name, so a boast of the land's yield becomes a founding story.

gains.a: the epithet in line 24-25 is shown to be an inherited Sangam formula, placing the epic's Puhar in the Chola praise tradition of Karikalan's city
gains.b: the idyll's unfailing river gains a myth of origin (Agastya's pot, the king's request) and a person who acts, which the idyll's description does not have

links.note: The narrator states as event that at the jewel seat Manimekalai came to know all her former births (பழம் பிறப்பு எல்லாம் ... உணர்ந்ததும்); in kaathai 27 she asks whether no one has known a former birth, and the materialist answers that such knowledge is the delusion of those led by a god or by dreams. The tension holds on the reading that 281-283 are the materialist's.
links.teaches: The materialist's dismissal names exactly the route by which the patikam says her knowledge came, a goddess carrying her to an island, so the epic lets the one school it answers attack the very ground of its heroine's conversion.

links.note: The patikam's line for kaathai 27 is that she asked them to state the faultless truth and heard (கேட்டதும்) the schools' doctrines; kaathai 27 lays the schools out one by one and she answers only the materialist.
links.teaches: The patikam's own word for the chapter of the schools is hearing, not defeating, which supports reading most of kaathai 27's accounts as reported views left for the Buddhist teaching of the later kaathais to answer.

links.note: Kural 225 ranks the strength of those who bear hunger below the strength of those who remove it; in the patikam the renunciant who begs with a bowl is the one who ends Kayachandigai's hunger-fire.
links.teaches: The Kural sets the one who endures hunger and the one who relieves it as two kinds of strength in rank, while the epic gives both to one person, a begging ascetic whose bowl feeds others, so its Buddhist renunciation removes the Kural's ranking rather than falling under it.

gains.a: the bowl scene gains a standard from the ethics books by which the heroine's begging is a higher strength than ascetic endurance, not a lower one
gains.b: the couplet's contrast between enduring and removing hunger is shown not to be exclusive, since a renunciant can hold both

links.note: Kural 362: if one must desire, desire not to be born, and that comes by desiring not to desire; the patikam closes with Manimekalai, having heard the dharma, vowing that becoming be cut off (பவத் திறம் அறுக என ... நோற்றதும்).
links.teaches: The Kural allows one desire, for birthlessness, and reaches it by turning desire on itself; the epic makes that one desire a vow kept with austerity after hearing a teacher, so the end the Kural states as inner paradox is reached in the epic through instruction and practice.

gains.a: the heroine's closing vow is seen to be the single desire the Kural permits, not a lapse from desirelessness
gains.b: the couplet's wish for birthlessness gains a path, a teacher's dharma and a vow, which the couplet does not name

new_concepts.gloss: the chaste wife whose virtue carries power
new_concepts.label_source: the verses use the word (பத்தினிப் பெண்டிர், line 64)

source_issues: Line 71 had a leftover HTML quote mark and line 78 an old-font vowel sign; both repaired in the core file, sense unaffected.
Lines 10 (கஞ்ச வேட்கையின் காந்த மன்) and 17 (ஆணு விசும்பின்) read oddly; the sense of the Kaveri's welcome at 17-18 is not certain.
